summary: This informational memo lists functional requirements for supporting MPLS traffic engineering across routing areas. Solutions defining procedures and protocol extensions for it are expected to meet these requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: A big network is divided into regions. This document lists what is needed for planning good paths across region borders.

subtitle: What a solution must do to let MPLS traffic engineering reach across IGP area boundaries without breaking routing hierarchy.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering worked only inside a single IGP area, because a head-end router sees only its own area and can no longer compute a constrained shortest path to a tail-end in another area.
tldr.mechanism: The memo states the problem, sets two key objectives (preserve the IGP hierarchy and scalability), and lists detailed MUST and SHOULD requirements for signaling, path computation, recovery and more.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements and evaluation criteria for solutions, not a protocol itself. Solutions that specify procedures and protocol extensions for inter-area MPLS TE are expected to satisfy them.

facts.label: Recovery on backup LSPs
facts.value: On the order of tens of msecs

today: RFC 4105 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and the registry metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements, not a protocol, so it is used as a checklist for solutions rather than something to implement directly.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE), defined using RSVP-TE and the OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions, is used by many network operators for goals such as measuring aggregated traffic, optimizing resource use, supporting end-to-end QoS guarantees, and fast recovery from link, node and Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) failures. Until now these mechanisms have been limited to a single Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) area.

This memo describes requirements for an inter-area MPLS TE mechanism that achieves the same goals across several IGP areas. Some requirements are mandatory (MUST) and others optional (SHOULD), because the needs of operators vary. A set of evaluation criteria for any solution is given at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators have a good way to steer traffic inside one region of a network. They now want the same steering across several regions, and this paper says what that must look like.

sections.title: How Intra-Area MPLS TE Works Today
sections.content:
The MPLS TE control plane sets up explicitly routed LSPs that follow a set of TE constraints. It has three components: a routing component that discovers the TE topology through link-state IGP extensions, a path computation component that places the LSP using a CSPF algorithm on the head-end, and a signaling component that establishes the LSP using RSVP-TE.

The memo lists uses of MPLS TE inside an area. Resource optimization moves aggregated flows away from over-utilized links, and traffic between two routers is easily measured by counting what is sent onto an LSP. For QoS, it can be combined with DiffServ, including DiffServ-Aware TE, to give per-class admission control. For recovery, backup LSPs allow traffic recovery on the order of tens of msecs, and Fast Reroute aims at sub-50ms recovery using either one-to-one detour LSPs or facility bypass LSPs.

Traffic can be directed into an LSP by static routing, IGP shortcuts, BGP recursive routing, or by advertising the LSP as a link into the IGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside one region, a planner can pick a route for traffic, reserve room for it, and prepare a spare route in case something breaks, all very quickly.

sections.title: The Inter-Area Problem and Key Objectives
sections.content:
The limit comes mainly from routing and path computation, not signaling. IGP hierarchy limits each head-end router's view to its own area, so it cannot run CSPF over the whole topology to find the shortest constrained path to a tail-end elsewhere. Operators with multi-area networks, or networks growing toward that, want inter-area resource optimization, inter-area QoS guarantees and fast recovery across areas, including recovery from Area Border Router (ABR) failures. A voice gateway example makes the point.

Running MPLS TE separately in each area is possible but weak. Traffic aggregation at ABRs gives sub-optimal resource use, no inter-area constrained shortest path or end-to-end QoS guarantee, and no local protection against ABR failure.

Two key objectives guide any solution. It MUST entirely preserve the concept of IGP hierarchy, so containment of routing information is not compromised. It also MUST preserve scalability: it must not make the IGP carry unreasonable extra information, must not unreasonably increase flooding frequency and must preserve RSVP-TE scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: Each region keeps its own map, so a router cannot see the whole trip. The fix must not make every region carry everyone else's map, or the network would get slow and messy.

sections.title: Signaling, Path Computation and Routing Requirements
sections.content:
A solution MUST interoperate with intra-area MPLS TE and allow provisioning at the head-end with end-to-end RSVP signaling, potentially with loose paths through the ABRs, without extra provisioning on the transit path. It MUST signal inter-area TE LSPs using RSVP-TE and let the head-end name LSRs, including ABRs, as strict or loose hops. It SHOULD allow excluding resources.

It SHOULD compute an optimal path across areas, meaning the shortest path under the IGP or TE metric, as a CSPF would find without multiple areas, but not every LSP needs an optimal path. Routing mechanisms MUST not alter IGP hierarchy, and a solution SHOULD avoid leaking dynamic TE topology across areas, even summarized. Path computation methods named include per-area computation by ERO expansion (with ABRs configured as loose hops or selected dynamically) and end-to-end computation through collaboration between ABRs. If more than one method is supported, the operator should choose per LSP.

Crankback MAY be supported and, if so, MUST be switchable per LSP via signaling; the memo notes it finds only a feasible path, and setup failures can grow as O(N^2). Diversely routed inter-area LSPs MUST be possible for link, node and SRLG diversity. For routing traffic into the LSP, a solution MUST support static routing and BGP recursive routing, while IGP shortcuts and advertising the LSP as an IGP link MUST be precluded when head-end and tail-end are in different areas.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner must be able to say which border gates to pass through, find a good route when it can, and still work with older equipment. Other rules keep the regions from sharing too much information.

sections.title: Reoptimization, Recovery and Other Requirements
sections.content:
A solution MUST support make-before-break reoptimization of an inter-area TE LSP when a better path appears in any traversed area, triggered by timer, event or manually. It SHOULD allow local reoptimization with the same set of ABRs, controlled by the head-end or an ABR, and MUST allow ABR control to be switched on or off per LSP via signaling. End-to-end reoptimization, which may change the transit ABRs, is head-end controlled.

Rerouting after SRLG, link or node failure or preemption MUST be supported. Fast recovery MUST be possible using the local protection of Fast Reroute, both for failures inside an area and for failure of an ABR, which typically carries a great deal of inter-area traffic. Because ABR protection with Fast Reroute needs a single end-to-end RSVP session, the solution MUST let signaling allow or preclude intra-area LSPs supporting an inter-area LSP.

Further requirements say a solution SHOULD satisfy the DS-TE requirements, SHOULD allow LSP nesting for hierarchy, SHOULD support hard and soft preemption, SHOULD allow auto-discovery of TE meshes across areas, and SHOULD support fault management such as LSP-PING and fault detection on backup LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: If a better road opens up, traffic should switch smoothly without a gap. If a border gate breaks, a ready-made detour should take over almost at once.

sections.title: Evaluation Criteria and Security
sections.content:
Solutions are evaluated on performance, complexity and backward compatibility. Performance criteria are the optimality of primary and backup paths in path cost, the ability to share bandwidth among inter-area backup LSPs protecting independent facilities, inter-area TE-LSP setup time in msec, and RSVP-TE and IGP scalability (state, number of messages, message size). A solution SHOULD NOT add so much complexity that it harms network stability.

For smooth migration, deployment SHOULD NOT affect existing MPLS TE, and the solution SHOULD allow setting up an inter-area LSP through transit LSRs that lack inter-area extensions. Extensions might be needed only on end-point LSRs, on ABRs and possibly on points of local repair protecting an ABR.

On security, the memo introduces no new issues beyond those inherent in MPLS TE and RSVP-TE. It stresses that changes to administratively configurable parameters should be made securely by authorized entities.
sections.plainLanguage: A good solution is judged by how good its routes are, how fast it sets them up, how simple it is, and whether older equipment can keep working alongside it.

viz.caption: THE THREE MPLS TE COMPONENTS (RFC 4105, SECTION 4.1)

items.title: Routing
items.text: Discovers the TE topology through link-state IGP extensions.

items.title: Path computation
items.text: Places the LSP on the head-end using CSPF over the TE topology and LSP constraints.

items.title: Signaling
items.text: Establishes the LSP with explicit routing, label distribution and resource reservation, using RSVP-TE.
